# Toward the conceptualization and measurement of transphobia-driven intimate partner violence

**Authors:** Beth J. Maclin; Sarah Peitzmeier; Natalie K. Krammer; Kieran P. Todd; Erin E. Bonar; Kristi E. Gamarel

**Affiliations:** aBehavioral & Community Health Sciences, School of Public Health, University of Pittsburgh, 130 De Soto St, Pittsburgh, PA, 15261, USA | bDepartment of Prevention and Community Health, Milken Institute School of Public Health, George Washington University, 950 New Hampshire Ave NW #2, Washington, DC, 20052, USA | cHealth Behavior and Biological Sciences, School of Nursing, University of Michigan, 426 N Ingalls St, Ann Arbor, MI, 48104, USA | dDepartment of Health Behavior and Health Education, School of Public Health, University of Michigan, 1415 Washington Heights, Ann Arbor, MI, 48109, USA | eCollege of Literature, Sciences, and the Arts, University of Michigan, 500 S State St #2005, Ann Arbor, MI, 48109, USA | fAddiction Center, Department of Psychiatry, University of Michigan Medical School, 2800 Plymouth Rd., Bldg. 16, Rm. 016-219W, Ann Arbor, MI, 48109, USA

## Abstract

Transgender and gender expansive (trans) people face high rates of violence, including unique forms of abuse from intimate partners that specifically leverage transphobia. Past qualitative studies have explored trans-specific intimate partner violence (IPV) and transgender IPV; we propose a new term, transphobia-driven IPV, investigated in this paper. The goals of this study were two-fold: (1) to qualitatively identify the subdomains and boundaries of transphobia-driven IPV with the explicit intention of new scale development; and (2) to examine the degree to which existing trans-focused IPV measurement scales adequately assess the construct. We recruited US-based, English-speaking trans survivors of IPV, aged 18 years and older, online through community-based organizations and Facebook/Instagram advertising. Twenty people participated in the study, of which 60 percent were white, 55 percent were assigned female at birth, and 60 percent were nonbinary. Through thematic analysis of the 20 in-depth interviews, we identified four subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV: pressure to perform, disrupting gender affirmation, belittling gender identity, and intentional misgendering. When examining nine existing screening tools and measures that ask about IPV related to the survivor’s trans identity, only one measure included questions related to all four subdomains. Further, the existing measures were either not psychometrically validated, only validated with a subpopulation of the trans community, or validated with a larger LGBTQ sample of which trans survivors comprised a small percentage. This study lays a foundation for new valid measures of transphobia-driven IPV that reflect the various ways in which transphobia can be leveraged by abusers and may be relevant across subpopulations of the trans community.

## Introduction

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines intimate partner violence as “behaviour by an intimate partner or ex-partner that causes physical, sexual or psychological harm, including physical aggression, sexual coercion, psychological abuse and controlling behaviours” (WHO, 2021). While this definition does not specify the gender of either the survivor or perpetrator, the majority of research to date focuses on the experiences of cisgender women in relationships with cisgender men (Bacchus et al., 2018; Donovan et al., 2016; Garcia-Moreno et al., 2005; McCarthy et al., 2018; Norlander and Eckhardt, 2005).

In response to the lived experiences of transgender, nonbinary, and gender expansive (referred to collectively as trans throughout manuscript) survivors, practitioners and researchers have identified the need to expand the conceptualization of who experiences IPV and screen for IPV among trans people, who, as a group, have been under-represented in IPV research to date (Das et al., 2022; Garthe et al., 2018; James et al., 2016; Peitzmeier et al., 2019; Peitzmeier et al., 2021; Valentine et al., 2017; Yerke and DeFeo, 2016). This shift has generated a growing evidence base regarding the IPV experiences of trans survivors, highlighting the increased risk this community faces. In the 2015 U.S. Transgender Survey, 54% of respondents reported lifetime IPV, and 44% reported some form of coercive control, including intimidation, emotional, and financial harm (James et al., 2016). Compared to cisgender individuals, a systematic review found that transgender individuals were 1.7 times more likely to experience any IPV, 2.2 times more likely to experience physical IPV, and 2.5 times more likely to experience sexual IPV (Peitzmeier et al., 2020). These data may be underestimated given the traditionally narrow definition of IPV rooted in cis- and hetero-normativity (Guadalupe-Diaz, 2019).

Growing research suggests that trans people are not only at greater risk of physical or sexual IPV as compared to cisgender individuals, but that they are also subject to unique forms of “trans-specific IPV” (Peitzmeier et al., 2021) due to the unique ways in which transphobia informs how IPV manifests for trans survivors. Guadalupe-Diaz (2019) describes how abusers, regardless of their own gender identity, may preferentially use abuse tactics that target the survivor’s trans identity because this both reinforces and is reinforced by societal genderism and transphobia. Examples of this kind of abuse include intentionally using the wrong pronouns, forcing the person to remain closeted, controlling their transition, and touching the person in a way that does not align with their gender (Cook-Daniels, 2015; Kurdyla, 2021; Messinger and Guadalupe-Diaz, 2020b). As cisgender survivors do not experience these manifestations of abuse and most IPV research focuses on and centers the experiences of cisgender survivors, general IPV screening tools miss key ways in which trans people may experience IPV.

We propose a new label for this phenomenon, transphobia-driven IPV, to replace previous terms used, including “trans-related IPV” (Peitzmeier et al., 2019), “trans-specific IPV” (Peitzmeier et al., 2021), and “transgender IPV” (Messinger and Guadalupe-Diaz, 2020a). “Trans--related IPV” and “trans-specific IPV” could inadvertently suggest that the abuse is the result of the person being trans or imply fault lies with the survivor. “Transgender IPV″ is often used as an umbrella term to refer to all types of IPV (e.g. physical, sexual, financial) experienced or perpetrated by trans people, and thus can create confusion when using it to refer specifically to transphobia-driven IPV, i.e. abuse experienced by a trans person, regardless of the gender of the perpetrator, in which the survivor’s trans identity is targeted in some way. This new framing of the phenomenon more accurately reflects not only that this is a type of IPV that happens specifically to trans people, but that it is also driven by how abusers are able to leverage transphobia to enhance the psychological impact and coercive control they enact on their partners.

In recent years, scholars have begun to articulate the boundaries and domains of transphobia-driven IPV via varied lenses. Quinn (2020) considers certain transphobia-driven IPV tactics to be examples of physical abuse (e.g., blocking transition-related care and recovery), financial abuse (e.g., not allowing the survivor to buy gender-related products), or isolation abuse (e.g., threatening to out the survivor as trans) while most other tactics often considered to be transphobia-driven IPV fall under a category of identity abuse. In Quinn’s conceptualization, transphobia-driven IPV is not a single latent construct but a constellation of tactics across different types of IPV. Koontz (2020) conceptualizes transphobia-driven IPV as consisting of two subdomains: “retroverting” (i.e., abuse tactics that force the survivor to regress back into or focus on the gender associated with their sex assigned at birth, e.g. intentionally misgendering someone) and “maneuverting” (i.e., abuse tactics that try to make the survivor’s affirmed gender seem unattainable in some way, either by sabotaging physical items the survivor needs to transition, or by saying a “real” man or woman would behave in a certain unattainable ideal way). While these processes of retroverting and maneuverting clarify how transphobia-driven IPV is related to the sociological process of “alter-casting” (i.e. how “Individual A can ‘cast’ Individual B … into a specific identity of Individual A’s choosing” (Koontz, 2020)), it is not clear how these categories map onto commonly measured domains of IPV (i.e., psychological, physical, sexual, and control) or whether these two categories have meaningful further subdomains within them.

The existing literature presents rich information on transphobia-driven IPV tactics and ways of understanding how and why these tactics are employed. However, none of the existing qualitative research was designed to inform scale development and measurement of transphobia-driven IPV. Thus, in this study, we sought to rigorously collect and analyze in-depth interviews from trans survivors of IPV, explicitly designing data collection and analysis to elicit the full breadth of transphobia-driven IPV, in order to inform scale development. In this paper, after positing our theoretical understanding of the boundaries and subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV, we examine how well existing measures capture the construct and propose a structure for future scale development based on this work.

## Materials and methods

### Participant recruitment

We recruited prospective participants online through community-based organizations and Facebook/Instagram advertisements between February 2020 and May 2021. Eligibility criteria included 1) being trans or gender expansive (i.e., defined as a difference in sex assigned at birth and current gender identity), 2) aged 18 years or older, 3) currently residing in the United States, 4) having access to a computer, tablet, or smartphone, 5) experiencing a romantic or intimate relationship that they felt was harmful, unsafe, and/or abusive in the past five years, and 6) being able to participate in the study in English. Of the 79 people who completed the eligibility screener, 77 were eligible to participate. Fifty-five people were contacted to complete an interview, of which 20 people accepted and did. We used purposive sampling methods to ensure a breadth of experiences were represented in the sample as we hypothesized that experiences might vary by participant gender, perpetrator gender, types of IPV reported in a brief screener, age, and race. We included 12 items adapted from IPV screeners (Peitzmeier et al., 2021; Smith et al., 1995) to assess physical IPV, sexual IPV, transphobia-driven IPV, and coercive control in the screener to purposively select participants who had experienced different types of IPV.

### Qualitative data collection

Twenty people completed interviews. Demographic data was collected with open-ended responses (e.g., “What are the primary word or words you would use to describe your racial/ethnic identity?” “What are the primary word or words you would use to describe your gender identity?” and “What is your sex assigned at birth, meaning the sex indicated on your original birth certificate?”). In-depth interviews were conducted via Zoom by KT, a trans/nonbinary interviewer, using an online Life History Calendar (LHC) method (Freedman et al., 1988).

LHC methods invite participants to co-create a timeline with an interviewer, enhancing recall over a defined period of time via a visual aid. We adapted the LHC for online delivery to sensitively elicit traumatic or difficult-to-recall events, and to understand how periods of violence overlapped with a participant’s gender journey or transition, perceived levels of safety over time while in the abusive relationship, and other important life events during the relationship that aided with recall. First, participants answered questions about their gender identity and what partners expected of them based on their gender presentation and identity using an interactive body-mapping activity adapted from Saint Arnault (2017). Second, participants were invited to create and mark a timeline that visually described the relationship, including markers for the beginning and end of the relationship, and important milestones or events that characterized the relationship for that participant (i.e., moving in together). This step created anchor points in the timeline to enhance recall of safety and harm during different periods of the relationship. Next, participants described the safety they felt at the different time points of their relationship and marked the timeline to indicate that, followed by the creation of a third layer on the online LHC that invited participants to place “harmful behavior tags.” We included 23 tactics as pre-created tags spanning physical, sexual, psychological, and transphobia-driven forms of IPV, drawn from validated IPV screening scales. Examples of pre-created tags include: shouting; slapping; threatened to hit or throw something; insisted on having sex; forced to have sex; destroying personal items; told that you are not a “real man” or a “real woman”; told not to ”act” trans or to behave more masculine or more feminine; told no one would want to be with someone who is transgender; intentionally being called by the wrong name or pronouns; and outed or threatened to out you to make you feel unsafe or ashamed. These were not intended to be an exhaustive list but rather to spur participants’ thinking across different domains of IPV. Participants were also provided with blank tags with an explicit invitation to create their own. Examples of participant-created tags include: gaslighting; comparing how much they loved me to what I was willing to do for them as a way to get me to do more; threatened children; threatened/actual self harm (in manipulative way); and financial control through lack of action. Finally at the end of the timeline creation, participants were asked to reflect on what memories, emotions, or reflections they felt in response to talking about the relationship felt like and the visuals they created. These visual methods create an opportunity to initially center the participant’s personhood and experience before diving into the actions of the perpetrator and resulting impact.

### Qualitative data analysis

Multiple members of the research team took part in a thematic analysis of the 20 interview transcripts. Two researchers (BM and KT) closely read a set of transcripts in order to independently develop codebooks of existing codes and sub-codes. They, along with SP, then reviewed and discussed the two codebooks in order to combine and refine the codes and sub-codes into a final comprehensive codebook.

BM and NK then coded the transcripts. To ensure consistent application of the codebook, these two researchers coded two transcripts in an iterative process. After each transcript, they discussed the consistencies and discrepancies with SP in order to come to a common understanding and use of the codebook. Through the process we refined the codebook further to address lack of clarity in any of the code definitions and to add new codes found in the transcripts that were not already represented. The remaining 18 transcripts were divided between BM and NK, who coded them independently, with regular meetings to discuss questions regarding the data and/or codebook.

A similarly collaborative and iterative process was undertaken to identify domains and subdomains within the realm of transphobia-driven IPV. BM and NK independently developed a schema representing the types of transphobia-driven IPV discussed by participants. They then compared and discussed the schemas in order to come to a consensus. The resulting schema was then further refined through discussion with SP to ensure specificity and distinction between each type of transphobia-driven IPV.

### Screening tool collection

We finalized our conceptual mapping of transphobia-driven IPV and then examined how existing measures tapped the subdomains we identified in the qualitative analysis. We sought to collect quantitative measures that were: 1) specific to trans populations or inclusive of trans people, and 2) included questions regarding IPV specifically linked to the survivor’s trans identity. We reviewed all articles collected in the systematic review by Peitzmeier et al. (2020). Additionally, an online search was conducted in March–April 2023 using PubMed and Google Scholar to capture more recent publications not included in the systematic review. References from the relevant articles identified in the systematic review and newly collected publications were reviewed to identify original source material and other screening tools that fit our inclusion criteria. Finally, we read two books and reviewed their references to identify additional screening tools (Guadalupe-Diaz, 2019; Messinger and Guadalupe-Diaz, 2020a). Once all of the measures were collected, each question was reviewed in relation to the qualitative subdomains to assess what types of transphobia-driven IPV were captured and what was missing.

### Ethical review

The Empower study was reviewed and approved by the University of Michigan Health Sciences and Behavioral Sciences Institutional Review Board. A data use agreement was established between the University of Michigan and the George Washington University.

### Positionality statement

Members of the research team hold various constellations of the following identities which are particularly relevant for this study: cisgender, femme, trans, transmasculine, nonbinary, woman, queer, straight, Asian, Black, multiracial, and white. Professionally, we are trained as psychologists, social and behavioral scientists, and victim advocates, and in qualitative and quantitative research methods. We include first-generation academics, and hold degrees ranging from the bachelor’s to the doctorate levels from U.S.-based universities. These various aspects of identity influenced the study conceptualization, analysis, and presentation of results. Of particular concern was the need to continually check the cis-normative thinking that all of us were socialized with to ensure that this work centers the experiences of trans people in their own right rather than in comparison to cisgender people.

## Results

### Study sample

Table 1 presents a summary of the 20 participants. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 63 years old, with most (n = 12) identifying as white. More than half (n = 11) of the participants were assigned female sex at birth. Regarding gender identity as participants described in their screening form: 10 were nonbinary, one was a nonbinary woman, one was a nonbinary femme, two were trans men, four were trans women, one was a trans female, and one was a transsexual woman.

### Manifestations of transphobia-driven IPV

The types of transphobia-driven IPV discussed by participants fit into two IPV domains: coercive control (i.e., isolation from social networks and restricting access to employment, education, financial resources, or medical care) and psychological abuse (i.e., insults, belittling, constant humiliation, intimidation, and threats of harm) (WHO, 2012). We found two subdomains within coercive control: pressure to perform and disrupting gender affirmation, and two within psychological abuse: belittling gender identity and intentional misgendering. Below we describe each subdomain, name common tactics, and present supporting quotes from participants.

#### Pressure to perform

The perpetrator seeks to pressure the survivor into performing the gender role associated with their sex assigned at birth. This type of abuse is related to everyday, smaller decisions made by the survivor, which can mean repeated, chronic exposure for the survivor. This can happen at any stage of gender affirmation. This form of abuse is largely centered on social dynamics, with the perpetrator being focused on how the survivor and their relationship is perceived by others. In some cases, the perpetrator appeared to find it easier to explain their relationship when their [survivor] partner fit into a specific gender-binary box. Common tactics include: demanding the survivor uses a deadname and/or the wrong pronouns; wears specific gendered clothing, hairstyles, or makeup that does not align with their communicated gender identity; and/or plays a gendered role within a relationship that does not align with their gender identity. Additionally, abusive partners may threaten to out the survivor if they do not comply with demands or attempt to end the relationship.

“I had to be a boyfriend to this person because they said that that was the only way that we could navigate the world safely and that was their decision that I had no say in … I was not allowed to go by my gender-neutral first name. They introduced me with the masculine [middle] name and that was the only name that was acceptable.”

“I feel like it was less outward, like you shouldn’t, like it was less trans-shaming but definitely, the expectation of presenting more femme in the beginning. I felt like I had to perform femininity I guess in the relationship that I was in.”

#### Disrupting gender affirmation

The perpetrator seeks to stop the survivor from engaging in behaviors, services, care, etc. that affirm their gender identity. This type of abuse is related to larger one-time or milestone decisions made by the survivor related to how they understand and present themselves. This type of abuse can occur across the spectrum of gender affirmation behaviors, from coming out to changing one’s appearance, pronouns, and/or name to seeking medical care and services. Because this abuse relates to defined decisions, it is less likely to be chronic and may stop after the survivor has made and acted upon the specific decision. Common tactics include: suggesting the decision is a mistake; destroying or hiding related tools, such as makeup, clothing, and/or medication; restricting access to gender affirming support systems, both people and services; and threatening to leave if the survivor pursues a specific type of gender affirmation (i.e. hormone replacement therapy, surgery).

“[My partner] did pressure me not to get bottom surgery. That was just a thing he did. He was very adamant about it …. He would pressure me to keep my penis, and I’m like, ‘Ew, bye. That’s not your decision.’ But he felt like he needed to voice his opinion, which I took into consideration.”

“So there’s a year gap, although I would have started ASAP and in that time, it was like, like I said, it was literally right after we got married that I realized. And so he was upset and at first I didn’t know if I could do anything. It’s like, ‘Well I’ll start hormones and we’ll just see how that goes, but I’d also want top surgery.’ And he was like, ‘I can’t deal with that.’ So that’s still a thing that has yet to be brought back up.”

#### Belittling gender identity

The perpetrator demeans the survivor directly, specifically with regard to their gender identity, or indirectly by targeting other trans people or the LGBTQ community. This type of abuse is frequently chronic, with the effect of chipping away at the self-esteem and self-perception of the survivor over time, creating a dependency on the abuser for feelings of security and/or validation. This is a way to trap the survivor in the relationship and/or to influence the survivor’s gender affirmation process. Common tactics include: saying ‘No one else will love you because you are trans’ and ‘You’re not a “real” woman or man’; questioning if the survivor is sure about their gender identity; and making derogatory comments about other trans people or the LGBTQ community.

“When I told my family and told her, and she definitely didn’t respond well, as I mentioned before. And that’s when a lot of the emotional abuse kind of revved up, telling me that no one would love me because I was a freak and also, included comments about my size and my weight.”

“And sometimes he would be completely disrespectful because I have a friend that I call my sister, and she’s transgender, too. However, her voice is as high as some women’s voices are. And so he would scream things up, say mean things about her, saying mean things about me and her. He wouldn’t believe that it was her over here, even think that I was just telling him that because there was a guy over here, which is extremely disrespectful to my sister. Because all she’s trying to do is have your back and my back because she loves me.”

#### Intentional misgendering

The perpetrator intentionally uses language that misgenders the survivor. This can be chronic or sporadic, depending on the intention of the perpetrator - either refusing to accept the gender identity of the survivor or punishing the survivor with hurtful language. Common tactics include: deadnaming; using the wrong pronouns; and using other gendered language in reference to the survivor that does not match their gender identity.

“Even the misgendering and the name for me, I think now, looking back at it, it was just always her little way of kind of like those little jabs … [It] started with just those little things and kind of went to other things from there … Sometimes it doesn’t seem like it’s that big at that moment, but I think in the long run, when they start to add up, it could be pretty big.”

“He was like, ‘You’re always trying to be somebody’s boss, you need to let me be the man, you need to let me be the man.’ And I was like, ‘Hold on.’ And I’m not gonna lie. I did let him know then, I’m not trying to be anybody’s man. And I don’t know why you use that phrase specifically knowing who you’re talking to.”

#### Co-occurrence

While these four subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV are distinct, participants detailed experiences that show how they sometimes co-occur. For example, belittling gender identity can be a tool to disrupt gender affirmation, such as telling a survivor that there was no point in having gender-affirming surgery because they will never be a “real” man or woman. Similarly, some abusive partners expressed disgust and/or animosity toward the larger LGBTQ community, including using derogatory terms or slurs; expressing dislike of related media or culture; and disapproving of the survivor’s LGBTQ friends or social groups. This served the purpose of indirectly communicating opposition to the survivor’s gender identity and affirmation (belittling gender identity) while also isolating the survivor from their LGBTQ peers and related gender affirming and support services (disrupting gender affirmation) by expressing opposition to their partner engaging with the LGBTQ community.

### Measures of IPV among LGBTQ survivors

We identified nine tools that specifically include questions related to transphobia-driven IPV (Brennan et al., 2012; Dyar et al., 2021; Garthe et al., 2018; James et al., 2016; Peitzmeier et al., 2019, 2021; Roch et al., 2010; Turell, 2000; Woulfe and Goodman, 2018). Table 2 presents the relevant items from these measures with a summary of how they map onto the four transphobia-driven IPV subdomains.

#### IPV screeners with transphobia-driven IPV questions

Turell (2000), Brennan et al. (2012), Garthe et al. (2018), and James et al. (2016) include 1–3 items relating to transphobia-driven IPV within a broader measure of IPV. They were not intended to comprehensively assess transphobia-driven IPV. Turell (2000) developed their survey based on “non-normed behavioral checklists of several local shelters for battered women” (p. 284). The question included by Brennan et al. (2012) was developed by their transgender advisory committee, but no details on the process are included in the manuscript. Garthe et al. (2018) references Wilson et al. (2009) as the source of the questions they used; however, Wilson et al. (2009) did not publish the specific questions included in their IPV victimization scale, which is why we assess Garthe et al. (2018) here. James et al. (2016) did not specify how they created the items related to transphobia-driven IPV, but described a collaborative, iterative process suggesting deductive strategies for their overall survey instrument. Three questions capture belittling gender identity (Garthe et al., 2018; James et al., 2016; Turell, 2000). Brennan et al. (2012) and James et al. (2016) capture disrupting gender affirmation. Garthe et al. (2018) captures pressure to perform. Intentional misgendering is missing.

#### Identity abuse measures for sexual and gender minorities (SGM)

Two papers present validated scales for measuring identity-related IPV among broader SGM populations. Neither of these measures are intended to be trans-specific and therefore exclude types of transphobia-driven IPV not experienced by cisgender sexual minoritized individuals.

Woulfe and Goodman (2018) validated a scale for measuring identity abuse among the LGBTQ community. The authors used deductive strategies to generate items through a review of the existing literature, followed by a review by five experts. They adapted work by Balsam and Szymanski (2005), which focused on lesbian and bisexual women, to be more inclusive of the entire LGBTQ community and to cover two themes found in the literature not covered in the Balsam and Szymanski scale. The four categories of LGBTQ-specific identity abuse they capture include: the threat of outing the survivor; belittling LGBTQ identity; using homophobic/transphobic language; and isolation from the LGBTQ community (Woulfe and Goodman, 2018). Four items capture belittling gender identity. One item captures pressure to perform. Intentional misgendering and disrupting gender affirmation are missing.

Dyar et al. (2021) validated three IPV measures for SGM populations. Of relevance for this analysis, they used deductive strategies to create a new measure of coercive control adapted from the Coercive Behaviors Sale (Frankland and Brown, 2014) and the 2010 National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey (Black et al., 2011), and a new measure of SGM-specific IPV focused on outing and social isolation. Within the SGM-specific IPV measure - the only measure with items related to transphobia-driven IPV - two items capture pressure to perform. Intentional misgendering, belittling gender identity, and disrupting gender affirmation are missing.

#### Transphobia-driven IPV scales

We found three scales specific to transphobia-driven IPV. Roch et al. (2010) include an eight-item measure for transphobic behaviors as a type of emotional abuse, but did not report how they generated the items. Three items capture belittling gender identity, and five capture disrupting gender affirmation. Intentional misgendering and pressure to perform are missing. Peitzmeier et al. (2019) validated a four-item measure for transphobia-driven IPV among transmasculine individuals. The items were generated using deductive strategies, including a literature review, with a focus on qualitative research, and a review of material from service organizations (Peitzmeier et al., 2019). One item captures belittling gender identity, two capture disrupting gender affirmation, and two capture pressure to perform; one of the questions combines both coercive control subdomains. Intentional misgendering is missing. Building from this scale through additional literature review and suggestions from participants and researchers, Peitzmeier et al. (2021) validated an expanded eight-item transphobia-driven IPV measure among transgender women. Two items capture pressure to perform, two capture disrupting gender affirmation, three capture belittling gender identity, and one captures intentional misgendering. While all four subdomains are reflected, certain nuances around hostility toward and isolation from the LGBTQ community and indirect misgendering are missing.

## Discussion

This study explicitly links the lived experiences of trans survivors of transphobia-driven IPV, a new term we propose, through original qualitative data with a consideration of existing IPV measures in order to identify gaps and inform future measures used by service providers and researchers. We identified four subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV and mapped them onto the broader IPV types of psychological abuse (belittling gender identity and intentional misgendering) and coercive control (pressure to perform and disrupting gender affirmation). Overall, the use of psychological abuse and coercive control serves to undermine the survivor’s sense of self, isolate them from their support systems, and increasingly tie their perceived value and safety to their abuser (Guadalupe-Diaz and Koontz Anthony, 2017; Guadalupe-Diaz, 2019; Koontz, 2020; Messinger and Guadalupe-Diaz, 2020b). Our data support the idea that transphobia-driven IPV is not a “new” type of IPV unrelated to other well-documented types of IPV, as the tactics we identified reflect psychological IPV and coercive control. However, our data also support that the tactics are unique when abusers leverage transphobia to enact psychological abuse and coercive control. Given how central gender identity is for one’s sense of self and how vulnerable one can feel while constructing and maintaining their identity through gender transition and affirmation, the tactics and impact (Stults et al., 2023; Taber et al., 2023) are distinct in ways that warrant a trans-specific screening tool.

While this analysis focuses on identifying the subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV, we also present tactics that typify each subdomain. Tactics identified in the in-depth interviews largely echo existing literature (Cook-Daniels, 2015; Guadalupe-Diaz, 2019; Kurdyla, 2021; Koontz, 2020; Messinger and Guadalupe-Diaz, 2020b; Quinn, 2020), suggesting saturation in the field and increasing confidence that the body of qualitative literature on transphobia-driven IPV has largely documented the breadth of transphobia-driven IPV tactics. Our participants, however, revealed certain nuances in tactics not reported before, including indirect misgendering and denigrating the trans and LGBTQ community. Indirect, rather than overt, methods of power and control can be harder to document, contest, and resist (Link and Phelan, 2014), creating unique challenges for the survivor to recognize, resist, and report abuse. It is also worth noting that one tactic identified elsewhere was not described in these interviews: transphobia-driven sexual abuse, including intentionally touching a survivor’s body in a way that conflicts with their gender identity (Cook-Daniels, 2015). While not to diminish or discredit survivors’ experiences of this type of IPV, past transphobia-driven IPV scale development work tested and ultimately dropped an item regarding transphobia-driven sexual abuse due to low item-total correlation, low factor loadings, and concerns that the item was not conceptually unique to transphobia-driven IPV and may be better categorized as a type of sexual IPV (Peitzmeier et al., 2021). Additional research may be needed to better understand how common this abuse tactic is and how it conceptually and psychometrically relates to the other well-documented tactics of transphobia-driven IPV. Overall, the tactics detailed here can be used for future item development as they cover the primary ways in which transphobia-driven IPV manifests.

Further, we examined published IPV measures that include questions related to transphobia-driven IPV to understand how well they capture the four subdomains of the construct. Only the eight-item measure by Peitzmeier et al. (2021) included items that reflect all four subdomains, though this measure could be further improved as it misses some tactics uncovered in this qualitative analysis and does not have an even distribution of items across the domains. Clarity on the boundaries of specific subdomains within a construct is also important, as including many more items from one subdomain relative to other subdomains in psychometric testing can unintentionally skew the entire item set away from the intended latent construct and toward the more specific subdomain, compromising unidimensionality of the scale. Inclusion of too many items from a specific subdomain can also artificially inflate the apparent correlation of items from that subdomain to the scale, making items from that subdomain incorrectly appear to have higher reliability than items from other subdomains (DeVellis and Thorpe, 2012).

Based on the approaches employed to develop these nine measures, one explanation for these gaps is the heavy reliance on deductive strategies. Best practices for scale development suggest that extensive qualitative and theoretical work should be done before generating potential scale items in order to fully map out all domains of a construct and, importantly, the boundaries of what is not included in a construct (DeVellis and Thorpe, 2012). Qualitative work that is explicitly designed to map out subdomains and generate potential items for scale development, as we have done in this paper, is also useful because DeVellis and Thorpe (2012) recommend starting with four times more items than you intend to retain in your final scale. Based on the methods described in the papers we reviewed, this type of exhaustive primary qualitative data collection and analysis and theoretical work designed explicitly for scale development was not conducted in conjunction with any existing transphobia-driven IPV scales.

Another explanation for the gaps we found is that some of the measures were either adapted from scales developed for non-trans populations and/or designed to include, but not focus on, trans survivors. In particular, using and adapting measures designed and validated for cisgender sexual minoritized populations will likely result in missing subdomains of how trans identity is targeted, manipulated, and controlled as this is not an aspect of identity abuse relevant for cisgender survivors (King et al., 2020). A crucial step when adapting existing measures is to assess if a concept or domain is missing to see if content validity holds for the new population or setting the measure is being adapted to (Stewart et al., 2012). Based on the review of the two SGM population-specific IPV measures (Dyar et al., 2021; Woulfe and Goodman, 2018), it is clear that a transphobia-driven domain is missing. This gap, however, is not surprising as neither intended to be specific to trans survivors. Woulfe and Goodman (2018) specifically noted that by recruiting an inclusive LGBTQ sample, they included historically ignored populations, but may have missed nuanced experiences for subgroups. They also highlighted the need for more intensive study of the experiences of identity abuse within each subpopulation to ensure each community’s experiences are captured (Woulfe and Goodman, 2018). Developing, validating, and using trans-specific measures that reflect the distinct experiences of trans survivors is critical to capture this population’s IPV exposure. We note that some researchers have started using a measure of transphobia-driven IPV with trans participants in conjunction with a broader LGBTQ identity abuse scale administered to all participants in samples of mixed cisgender and trans SGM individuals in order to capture a full range of abuse experiences (Stults et al., 2023; Taber et al., 2023).

We also found that no existing scale has been psychometrically validated in a large diverse sample of trans survivors: Peitzmeier et al. (2021) was validated only with transgender women (though a subset of items was previously tested with transmasculine individuals (Peitzmeier et al., 2019)); Dyar et al. (2021) was validated in a sample that was 23.7 percent transmasculine or nonbinary-assigned female at birth; and Woulfe and Goodman (2018) was validated in a sample that was 19.3 percent trans. These sample demographics mean that the psychometric performance of these scales is largely driven by how they perform in cisgender sexual minoritized populations or in a subset of trans populations; their performance across trans communities is unclear.

In practice, IPV screening in different contexts may have different objectives. For instance, screening in primary care settings may require a very brief screener in order to be feasible for use in a 15-min appointment. However, domestic violence service providers may benefit from a more detailed assessment that provides more comprehensive coverage of tactics across subdomains so that specific support services can be tailored to the particular tactics used. Screening for research purposes may depend on the focus of the study and relative participant burden across assessments. Given these different contexts, there is unlikely to be one single scale that is best for use across all settings. Nonetheless, the goal of our work is to inform the development of future behavioral IPV screeners and assessments in this population by identifying key subdomains. Based on our review of the literature, to our knowledge, only one existing scale covers each of these subdomains and has been validated with samples of transmasculine individuals and transgender women (Peitzmeier et al., 2021). However, future research is warranted to improve this scale with additional items, particularly related to intentional misgendering, so that there is adequate representation of items across subdomains. Finally, those screening for IPV in trans populations should note that measures assessing physical, sexual, or other forms of IPV are needed to fully screen for IPV in addition to a measure focused on transphobia-driven IPV. While transphobia-driven IPV tends to be the most common type of IPV, one study found that only 15.5% of transfeminine survivors reported physical or sexual IPV alone without also reporting any transphobia-driven IPV (Peitzmeier et al., 2021). Further, estimates suggest that up to 50% of Black transgender women experience physical or sexual IPV in their lifetime (James et al., 2016, Bukowski et al., 2018), underscoring the importance of comprehensive screening for IPV to ensure survivors are not missed based on a narrow approach to IPV assessment.

### Strengths and limitations

This study expands upon the pioneering qualitative work of Guadalupe-Diaz (2019) describing transphobia-driven IPV by: 1) leveraging insights on the nature of transphobia-driven IPV to create the first study that was explicitly designed to inform inductive scale item generation for better measurement of transphobia-driven IPV, and 2) through the application of current innovative technology-mediated qualitative methods. This study leveraged Zoom to have face-to-face online interviews with an interactive LHC method integrated into the interview (Freedman et al., 1988; Gray et al., 2020). This method helped participants visually and verbally organize the trajectory of their abusive relationship, including how acts of abuse were timed in relation to their gender affirmation journey and promoting recall. We further coded and analyzed the data collaboratively with at least two team members actively involved in each stage of work to enhance dependability.

The participants were recruited and interviewed online, which means their experiences may not be reflective of the general trans adult population in the US. Future research should use a variety of recruitment and data collection modalities - online and in person - in order to expand access and inclusion for participants excluded from this study.

The evaluations of the existing transphobia-driven IPV items and measures are based on what the respective authors published regarding the sources of the survey questions and development of their measures. It is possible that other strategies were employed in developing items that were not included in available publications. However, the gaps in content validity between the evaluated measures and the qualitative subdomains we identified remain.

## Conclusion

This study identifies four subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV based on 20 in-depth qualitative interviews with trans survivors, one of the largest sets of qualitative interviews to our knowledge that has been conducted to date on this topic. These interviews were also the first specifically designed to lay the groundwork for rigorous inductive scale development. Future measures for assessing transphobia-driven IPV can enhance content validity and rigor through testing a large item pool that is representative of all four subdomains of transphobia-driven IPV within a sample that reflects the diversity of gender, race, ability, class, and other identities within the broad trans community.

# The Current State of Sexual Fluidity Research

**Authors:** Sabra L. Katz-Wise; Kieran P. Todd

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Adolescent/Young Adult Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 2Department of Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Sexual fluidity research (i.e., change over time in one or more sexual orientation dimensions) has grown exponentially, with advancements in conceptual models, measurement, and understanding of sexual orientation as a construct and developmental process that accommodates potential for change. Sexual fluidity research has also moved beyond samples of white cisgender women to consider the experiences of individuals with other sociodemographic characteristics and has examined change across multiple dimensions of sexual orientation, mechanisms of change, and associations with health outcomes. This review provides a brief narrative of historical conceptualizations of sexual orientation and fluidity and the current state of research on sexual fluidity. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research, policy, and clinical practice.

In recent years, sexual fluidity research has increased, necessitating an evaluation of the current state of research and opportunities for additional exploration and advancement in this field. In this article, we first provide a brief overview of historical conceptualizations of sexual orientation and sexual fluidity (i.e., sexual orientation change over time). Then we review the current state of sexual fluidity research and limitations of research to date on this topic. Finally, we offer recommendations for future research, policy, and practice.

## Research on Sexual Orientation and Sexual Fluidity Prior to 2011

The models that define sexual orientation have changed over time, alongside the research methodologies and implications for people who embody one or more sexual orientations. Sexual orientation has historically been defined within a binary model of two different types of people who are characterized by their sexual attractions (homosexual versus heterosexual) [1, 2]; in later years, bisexuality was added to this model. Known as the “master narrative” of sexual orientation, this dual model has been used to create static categories that do not consider the processes of sexual orientation development that instead posit a more fluid model of development that allows for changes in sexual orientation over time. Sexual orientation, in this model, develops early, in the same way for all sexual minorities (i.e., developing sexual orientation/identities at the same age in the same manner), and remains stable over the life course. Challenging this category-driven model, Diamond offered an alternative model. The “capacity for situation-dependent flexibility in sexual responsiveness”, which allows individuals to experience changes in sexual desire across both short-term and long-term periods, requires a model that is more dynamic than the “master narrative” [3]. Sexual fluidity explains that for some individuals, sexual orientation is not fixed and can be prompted to change by a variety of situational, interpersonal, and societal factors.

The advent of sexual fluidity research originated from the need to move past a static view of sexual orientation and was a response to a cisgender male-centered framework for understanding sexual orientation development. Before the 21st century, much like all human research, sexual orientation was studied primarily in men, with any frameworks and findings applied to women without studying them directly. In the late 1990s and beyond, Diamond’s research introduced the concept of sexual fluidity to push against narratives of static sexual orientation, while also centering women’s experiences.

Sexual fluidity research has been primarily conducted within the field of psychology, with some work done in sociology and public health. Notably, Baumeister’s research on female sexuality and “Differential Erotic Plasticity” asserted that compared to men: 1) women’s sexual histories should be more variable, 2) women are more influenced by sociocultural factors (e.g., culture, religion, peer influences), and 3) women have more “malleable behaviors” and thus are more likely to be more fluid in their sexuality over their life course [4]. Similarly, a study that evaluated sexual fluidity in three dimensions of sexual orientation (sexual fantasy, romantic attraction, and sexual behavior) in gay, straight, and bisexual men and women found gender differences, whereby women self-reported a greater change in their sexual orientation over time than men [5].

## Sexual Fluidity Research in the Past Decade

The past decade (2011–2021) has seen an increase in research on sexual fluidity, with studies expanding on prior research in several key areas. First, this research has expanded the definition and types of sexual fluidity and considered the experiences of cisgender men and transgender and nonbinary (TNB) individuals, in addition to cisgender women. Second, recent research has examined fluidity in more than one sexual orientation dimension (i.e., attractions, identity, or behavior/gender of sexual partners), and begun to examine patterns of sexual fluidity beyond frequency with which sexual fluidity occurs. Third, this research has explored mechanisms and predictors of sexual fluidity to better understand why and when sexual fluidity occurs. Finally, this research has examined links between sexual fluidity and health outcomes.

### Sexual Fluidity Among Different Populations

Research in the past decade has moved beyond the conceptualization of sexual fluidity as only change in attractions [1] to change in any dimension of sexual orientation [6–8]. In recent years, research has also started exploring different types of sexual fluidity among women, such as situational attractions and discordance between attractions and sexual partners [9]. It has also become more common for research to examine sexual fluidity in cisgender men, as well as TNB people, though some recent studies have still focused on cisgender women [10, 11]. Research that has included both cisgender women and men has provided an opportunity to examine gender differences in sexual fluidity frequency. This research has yielded mixed results, with some confirming earlier assumptions that cisgender women are more sexually fluid than cisgender men, and other research finding no gender difference, particularly among sexual minorities [12]. This research has also found that in general, sexual minorities are more sexually fluid than heterosexual individuals [6, 13], and that sexual fluidity is more common among adolescents than among young adults or adults [6], though individuals can be sexually fluid throughout adulthood [14]. Within sexual minorities, individuals with a plurisexual identity (i.e., orientation toward more than one gender; e.g., bisexual) are more likely than lesbian and gay individuals to be sexually fluid [13, 15]. Prior research has also found that TNB individuals have a high frequency of reporting sexual fluidity [16], with transgender men more likely than cisgender individuals to report sexual fluidity [17].

### Change Across Sexual Orientation Dimensions

Although much of sexual fluidity research has been limited to one dimension of sexual orientation, more recently, research in this area has considered fluidity in multiple dimensions of sexual orientation. We identified three studies that examined sexual fluidity in all three primary dimensions of sexual orientation (identity, attractions, and behavior), two among adolescents and young adults [7, 8] and one among individuals in early to mid-adulthood [6]. One adolescent study found that frequency of sexual fluidity differed by dimension; for example, 26% of girls and 11% of boys reported identity fluidity, whereas 31% of girls and 10% of boys reported attraction fluidity [8]. Following the lead of prior research [3], sexual fluidity research has continued to move beyond the examination of sexual fluidity frequency among different groups to patterns of sexual fluidity, such as directionality (i.e., toward sexual minority orientation, toward heterosexual orientation, or within sexual minority orientation) [18–21].

### Mechanisms and Factors Related to Sexual Fluidity

Research in the past decade has continued to examine mechanisms of and factors related to sexual fluidity. One study used qualitative interview data to develop the facilitative environments model, a theoretical framework of sexual fluidity as occurring at the confluence of multiple factors on individual, interpersonal, and societal levels [22]. Two studies examined attitudes and beliefs related to sexual fluidity, finding that fluidity in attractions was linked to attitudes toward bisexuality and beliefs about sexuality as changeable and influenced by one’s environment, particularly among sexual minority women [23, 24]. Two recent studies examined the role of religiosity in sexual fluidity, with one study finding that religiosity was not associated with changes in attractions over time among adolescents [25], and another study finding that more religiosity was associated with greater fluidity in sexual orientation identity among adults [26]. Another recent direction has been the examination of the role of genetics and how they work in tandem with environmental factors to create the conditions under which sexual fluidity may occur [2]. Notably, genetics cannot offer a full explanation for sexual fluidity, but rather must be considered alongside other contextual factors.

### Sexual Fluidity and Health

The final area in which sexual fluidity research has expanded in the past decade is health outcomes. This research has generally found that sexual fluidity is linked to more adverse health outcomes, including greater depression, greater substance use, and higher body mass index [18, 19, 27–30]. Studies examining links between directionality of sexual fluidity and mental health have yielded different results by gender and health outcome. In one study, only fluidity toward a sexual minority identity was associated with greater substance use among boys, but fluidity in any direction (toward heterosexual, toward sexual minority, multidirectional) was associated with greater substance use among girls [21]. Another study found that identity fluidity was differentially linked to body mass index and physical activity levels, depending on the direction of the change; for example, men who reported fluidity toward a sexual minority identity had a lower BMI and greater physical activity, whereas men who reported fluidity toward a heterosexual identity had the opposite pattern [19]. Two additional studies examined associations between sexual fluidity and health among transgender individuals, finding that attraction fluidity was associated with increased risk for adverse mental health outcomes among transgender adults [31] and identity fluidity was associated with more adverse mental health outcomes among transgender men [17]. Notably, these studies have been limited to the examination of fluidity in just two sexual orientation dimensions: sexual orientation identity and attractions; to our knowledge, no research has examined how fluidity in sexual behavior is associated with health outcomes.

## Prior Limitations and Recommendations for Future Research on Sexual Fluidity

Prior research on sexual fluidity has been limited in several ways, related to sampling, measurement and study design, and implications of sexual fluidity on individual health behaviors and outcomes. In terms of sampling, previous sexual fluidity research has typically been conducted with samples that are cisgender and white race/ethnicity. Although some research has examined sexual fluidity among TNB people [16], more research is needed to fully understand sexual orientation changes among this population. Another important area for future research is patterns of sexual fluidity by race/ethnicity, as social and cultural norms and beliefs about sexual orientation may affect whether and when sexual fluidity occurs. Qualitative methods may be particularly useful in understanding how these factors may relate to sexual fluidity in different race/ethnicity groups.

In terms of measurement, much of prior sexual fluidity research has been limited in considering fluidity in only one sexual orientation dimension, though a small number of studies have examined multiple dimensions [6–8]. It is critical to examine fluidity in multiple dimensions of sexual orientation, as these dimensions are not always aligned within an individual person at any given time point [32, 33] and thus there may be differences in how and whether each of these dimensions change over time. More research is needed on patterns of change across sexual orientation dimensions, such as whether dimensions change simultaneously or sequentially. It will also be important for sexual fluidity research to measure change both retrospectively (i.e., reflecting on past change) and prospectively (i.e., reporting change over time, such as measuring current sexual orientation identity at multiple time points in a longitudinal study). Finally, more research is needed to understand whether and how sexual fluidity – particularly fluidity in sexual partner gender – is related to both health behaviors and mental and physical health outcomes.

## Implications for Policy and Practice

Specific research questions and methodologies are not only important for increasing our knowledge about sexual orientation, they are also necessary for informing policy and clinical practice, such as sexual and reproductive health care, which can be better tailored to specific patients if clinicians are informed and knowledgeable about sexual fluidity and related outcomes. First, a better sense of who is a part of the sexual minority community is required, demanding explicit and thorough measurement of sexual orientation both in US population-level surveys, as well as in clinical intake and assessments. Such measurement should be rigorous and ideally assessed at multiple time points over the life course to ensure accurate collection of sexual orientation data and to provide affirming care for all individuals. Accurate assessment of sexual orientation is especially relevant for sexual health care in youth. If we can more accurately assess and understand sexual fluidity in youth, we can better advocate for inclusive comprehensive sexuality education that provides young people with the tools they need to have safer sex, regardless of the gender of their sexual partner(s). More broadly, accurate assessment of sexual orientation can inform clinical care of individuals of all ages, better ensuring that all individuals have access to affirming medical and mental health care.
